HomeGuide's 2026 ranges put standard tank replacement at $600-$3,100 and tankless installation at $1,400-$5,600. -> Heat pump installs need a fit check. The IRS page reviewed for this build says the credit applied through December 31, 2025. How to use this guide before you call The fastest way to get a useful quote is to describe the job as a scope, not as a product purchase. 1. Identify the current setup Note whether the existing heater is gas, electric, tankless or heat pump. Add the approximate age if you know it, the install location, and the symptom that triggered the replacement conversation. That gives the plumber a starting point before they see the site. 2. Decide whether this is like-for-like If the new heater keeps the same broad type, fuel and location, compare it first against the standard replacement band. If the job changes heater type or building services, compare it as a conversion. That framing makes the HomeGuide ranges more useful. 3. Ask the permit question early Do not wait until the day of install to ask who handles permits. Oregon's guidance shows that water heater replacement can be permit-required plumbing work. Your local answer may differ, so ask who checks it and who schedules inspection if one is needed. 4. Treat incentives as current-only If a heat pump recommendation depends on a rebate or credit, verify the current program before you accept the payback. The IRS source reviewed for this guide documents the federal credit through December 31, 2025, so a 2026 claim needs fresh proof. Quote script "I have a [gas/electric/tankless/heat pump] water heater in [garage/basement/closet/utility room]. I want to know whether this is a like-for-like replacement, repair, or conversion.
